data: © NASA/JPL-Caltech — Gusev Crater landing site; rover stuck 2009, last contact 2010.

Mars Exploration Rover A. Designed for a 90-sol primary mission; lasted 2,208 sols. Discovered evidence that Gusev Crater had once held volcanic-water interaction. Got stuck in soft soil at "Troy" in 2009; the team kept Spirit running as a stationary platform until the last contact in March 2010.
First long-distance Mars rover; demonstrated multi-year robotic geology on the Martian surface.

Spirit landed in Gusev Crater on January 4, 2004 — three weeks before its twin Opportunity touched down on the opposite side of Mars. Designed for 90 sols, Spirit operated for 6 years and traversed 7.7 km until its wheels became permanently mired in soft soil at "Troy". From a stranded rover, it continued as a stationary science platform until contact was lost in March 2010.
Mars Exploration Rover during integration — 185 kg, 6 wheels, Pancam mast camera, RAT rock-abrasion tool.
Winter Haven at McMurdo, sols 814-980 (2006) — Pancam 360° panorama. The Columbia Hills, named for the lost STS-107 crew, dominate the horizon.
Spirit's Troy stuck-rover site, captured by MRO HiRISE after wheel embedment in May 2009.
Drilling at the Adirondack rock, sol 34 — first use of the rock-abrasion tool on Mars.
Climbing Husband Hill, finding silica at Home Plate
Silica-rich soil exposed by Spirit's broken right-front wheel at Home Plate — evidence of past hydrothermal activity in Gusev Crater.
Sunset over Gusev Crater photographed by Pancam, sol 489 (May 19 2005). One of the iconic blue-tinged Martian dusk images.
Orrery reference map of CTX imagery and the Spirit traverse data

Illustrated block map of Spirit’s route across Gusev Crater, 2004–2010: from the landing site (sol 0) past Bonneville Crater (sol 66), Columbia Hills (sol 159) and the Hills summit (sol 581) to Home Plate (sol 744) and the rover’s final position (sol 2210).
